We state the first main result of this section. Let A and $A^{\prime}$ be equivalent quasi-bialgebras with a gauge transformation F on $A^{\prime}$ and an isomorphism $\alpha:A\to A_{F}^{\prime}$ of quasi-bialgebras. The map $\alpha$ induces a strict tensor functor $(\alpha^{*}$ ,id,id) from $A_{F}^{\prime}$ -Mod to A-Mod as explained in Example 2 of XI.4 Since $\alpha$ is an isomorphism, $\alpha^{*}$ is a tensor equivalence.
Theorem XV.3.5. The tensor functor $(\alpha^{*},\mathrm{id},\varphi_{2}^{F})$ is a tensor equivalence between $A^{\prime}$ -Mod and A-Mod.

Proof. Replacing $F$ by $F^{-1}$ which is another gauge transformation, we get a tensor functor (id, id, $\varphi_{2}^{F^{-1}}$ ) from $A_{F}^{\prime}$ -Mod to $A^{\prime}$ -Mod which turns out to be an inverse to (id, id, $\varphi_{2}^{F}$ ). The tensor functor $(\alpha^{*},$ id, $\varphi_{2}^{F}$ ) is the composition of the tensor equivalence (id, id, $\varphi_{2}^{F}$ ): $A^{\prime}$ -Mod $\rightarrow$ $A_{F}^{\prime}$ -Mod and of the tensor equivalence $(\alpha^{*},$ id, id).

## XV.4 Braid Group Representations

Let $(A, \Delta , \varepsilon , \Phi , R)$ be a braided quasi-bialgebra with trivial unit constraints, $V$ a left $A$-module, and $n$ an integer $> 1$. We recall from Chapters X and XIII how to define a representation of the braid group $B_{n}$ on $V^{\otimes n}$. Since $\Phi$ is not necessarily trivial, we have to make precise what we mean by $V^{\otimes n}$.

Let us place ourselves in the general situation where we have a braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ with associativity constraint a and braiding c. In XI.5 we constructed a strict tensor category $\mathcal{C}^{str}$ which is tensor equivalent to $\mathcal{C}.$ The tensor product of $\mathcal{C}^{str}$ is denoted *. By definition, we set $V^{\otimes n}=V^{*n}$ , which means that $V^{\otimes n}$ is equipped with the unique system of parentheses opening only at the extreme left. For instance, we have $V^{\otimes 4}=((V\otimes V)\otimes V)\otimes V.$ Define automorphisms $c_{1},\dots,c_{n-1}$ of $V^{\otimes n}=V^{*n}$ in $\mathcal{C}^{str}$ by

$$
c _ {i} = \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {*} (i - 1)} * c _ {V, V} * \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {*} (n - i - 1)}.
$$

$$
c _ {i} = \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {*} (i - 1)} * c _ {V, V} * \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {*} (n - i - 1)}.
$$

By Theorem XIII.1.3 and Corollary X.6.9 we know that there exists a unique morphism of groups $\rho_{n}^{\mathcal{C}}:B_{n}\rightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(V^{\otimes n})$ sending the generator $\sigma_{i}$ of $B_{n}$ to $c_{i}$ for any $i=1,\dots,n-1.$ The representation $\rho_{n}^{\mathcal{C}}$ will be called the braid group representation associated to the braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}.$ We now make $c_{i}$ explicit in terms of the original category $\mathcal{C}.$

$$

Proof. This follows from Relation (XI.5.4) which expresses the tensor product of morphisms in the strict category $\mathcal{C}^{str}$ in terms of the tensor product of morphisms and of the associativity constraint in $\mathcal{C}$ . We also use Relation (XI.5.3) in the following special cases:

$$

Let $A^{\prime}=\left(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime},\varepsilon^{\prime},\Phi^{\prime},R^{\prime}\right)$ be another braided bialgebra. We assume that $A$ and $A^{\prime}$ are equivalent braided quasi-bialgebras in the sense of Definition 3.8, i.e., there exist a gauge transformation $F$ on $A^{\prime}$ and an isomorphism $\alpha:A\to\left(A^{\prime}\right)_{F}$ of braided quasi-bialgebras. In particular, we have

$$
F _ {2 1} R ^ {\prime} F ^ {- 1} = (\alpha \otimes \alpha) (R).
$$

(4.3)

For any integer $n > 1$ we have two braid group representations $\rho_{n}^{A},\rho_{n}^{A^{\prime}}:B_{n}\to \operatorname{Aut}(V^{\otimes n})$ associated to A and $A^{\prime}$ respectively and acting on the same space. The main result of this section asserts that these representations are equivalent.

Theorem XV.4.2. Let A and $A^{\prime}$ be equivalent braided quasi-bialgebras. With the previous notation, we have

$$
\rho_ {n} ^ {A ^ {\prime}} (g) (w) = F _ {1 2} ^ {- 1} \rho_ {n} ^ {A} (g) \left(F _ {1 2} w\right)
$$

for all $g \in B_{n}$ and $w \in V^{\otimes n}.$

Proof. By Theorem 3.9, we know that both braid group representations are equivalent. It is therefore enough to compute the equivalence on one special element of the braid group. We choose the generator $\sigma_{1}$ . By (4.1) and (4.3) we have for $v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\in V$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {n} ^ {A ^ {\prime}} \left(\sigma_ {1}\right) \left(v _ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes v _ {n}\right) = \left(R _ {1 2} ^ {\prime} \left(v _ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes v _ {n}\right)\right) _ {2 1} \\ = \left(\left(F _ {2 1} ^ {- 1} (\alpha \otimes \alpha) (R) F _ {1 2}\right) \left(v _ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes v _ {n}\right)\right) _ {2 1} \\ = F _ {1 2} ^ {- 1} \left((\alpha \otimes \alpha) (R) \left(F _ {1 2} \left(v _ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes v _ {n}\right)\right)\right) _ {2 1} \\ = F _ {1 2} ^ {- 1} \rho_ {n} ^ {A} \left(\sigma_ {1}\right) \left(F _ {1 2} \left(v _ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes v _ {n}\right)\right). \\ \end{array}
$$

It should be clear that the statement of Theorem 4.2 depends on the way we put parentheses on $V^{\otimes n}$ . Other systems of parenthesizing give rise to different, but equivalent braid group representations.

## XV.5 Quasi-Hopf Algebras

For the sake of completeness we introduce quasi-Hopf algebras as defined by Drinfeld [Dri89b]. As above, all quasi-bialgebras considered here have trivial unit constraints, i.e., $l=r=1.$

Definition XV.5.1. A quasi-bialgebra $(A, \Delta ,\varepsilon ,\Phi)$ is a quasi-Hopf algebra if there exist an invertible anti-automorphism S of the algebra A and elements $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of A such that for all elements a in A we have

$$
\sum_ {(a)} S \left(a ^ {\prime}\right) \alpha a ^ {\prime \prime} = \varepsilon (a) \alpha , \quad \sum_ {(a)} a ^ {\prime} \beta S \left(a ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = \varepsilon (a) \beta ,
$$

(5.1)

and

$$
\sum_ {i} X _ {i} \beta S \left(Y _ {i}\right) \alpha Z _ {i} = 1, \quad \sum_ {i} S \left(\bar {X} _ {i}\right) \alpha \bar {Y} _ {i} \beta S \left(\bar {Z} _ {i}\right) = 1
$$

(5.2)

where $\Phi=\sum_{i} X_{i}\otimes Y_{i}\otimes Z_{i}$ and $\Phi^{-1}=\sum_{i} \bar{X}_{i}\otimes \bar{Y}_{i}\otimes \bar{Z}_{i}$ . A quasi-Hopf algebra is braided if the underlying quasi-bialgebra is.

We shall write $( A, \Delta, \varepsilon, \Phi, S, \alpha, \beta)$ to express the complete data of a quasiHopf algebra. As in XIV.2 consider the category $A\text{-}Mod_{f}$ of left $A$ -modules that are finite-dimensional vector spaces over the ground field k. Equip it with the tensor category structure induced by $\Delta$ and $\Phi$ . For any object V of $A\text{-}Mod_{f}$ consider the objects $V^{*}$ and $^{*}V$ as defined in Example 1 of XIV.2. We define maps $b_{V}: k \to V \otimes V^{*}$ , $d_{V}: V^{*} \otimes V \to k$ , $b_{V}^{\prime}: k \to^{*}V \otimes V$ , and $d_{V}^{\prime}: V \otimes^{*}V \to k$ by

$$
b _ {V} (1) = \sum_ {i} \beta v _ {i} \otimes v ^ {i}, \quad d _ {V} \left(v ^ {i} \otimes v _ {j}\right) = < v ^ {i}, \alpha v _ {j} >,
$$

$$
b _ {V} ^ {\prime} (1) = \sum_ {i} v ^ {i} \otimes S ^ {- 1} (\beta) v _ {i}, d _ {V} ^ {\prime} \left(v _ {i} \otimes v ^ {j}\right) = < S ^ {- 1} (\alpha) v _ {i}, v ^ {j} >
$$

where $\{v_{i}\}_{i}$ is a basis of V and $\{v^{i}\}_{i}$ the corresponding dual basis.

## XV.7 Notes

Quasi-bialgebras, quasi-Hopf algebras, and gauge transformations were invented by Drinfeld [Dri89b][Dri90][Dri89c] in relation with his treatment

of the monodromy of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equations (to be considered in Chapter XIX). Drinfeld used the term "quasi-triangular quasi-bialgebra" for a braided quasi-bialgebra. In [Dri89b], Section 1, Drinfeld showed that one always could reduce a general quasi-Hopf algebra to a quasi-bialgebra with $l=r=1.$

Altschuler and Coste [AC92] proved (see Exercise 5) that in any braided quasi-Hopf algebra the square of the antipode is an inner automorphism (just as for braided Hopf algebras, c.f. VIII.4). They also defined ribbon quasi-Hopf algebras generalizing the ribbon algebras of XIV.6. The braided quasi-Hopf algebra $D^{\omega}(G)$ of Section 5 is due to Dijkgraaf, Pasquier, and Roche [DPR90] and was shown in [AC92] to be a ribbon quasi-Hopf algebra. Let us remark that when the 3-cocycle $\omega$ is changed by a coboundary, then $D^{\omega}(G)$ is changed by a gauge transformation, so that the tensor category of modules of $D^{\omega}(G)$ depends on the cohomology class of $\omega.$

Exercise 1 is taken from [Res90] while Exercise 4 is from [Dri89b].

Indeed, take an infinite family $(e_{n})_{n\in\mathbf{N}}$ of linearly independent vectors; then the element $\sum_{n\geq0} e_{n}h^{n}$ of $V[[h]]$ does not belong to $V \otimes\mathbf{C}[[h]]$ .

## XVI.3 Topological Tensor Product

Let M and N be left modules over the algebra $K=\mathbf{C}[[h]]$ . Consider the $K$ -module $M\otimes_{K}N$ obtained as the quotient of the vector space $M\otimes N$ by the subspace spanned by all elements of the form $fm\otimes n-m\otimes fn$ where f belongs to K, m to M, and n to N.

Definition XVI.3.1. The topological tensor product $M \widetilde{\otimes} N$ of $M$ and $N$ is the h-adic completion of $M \otimes_{K} N$ :

$$
M \widetilde {\otimes} N = \left(M \otimes_ {K} N\right) ^ {\sim} = \lim _ {n > 0} \left(M \otimes_ {K} N\right) / h ^ {n} \left(M \otimes_ {K} N\right).
$$

Since it is defined as a completion, the topological tensor product of two modules is always complete. Given $m\in M$ and $n\in N$ we denote by $m\widetilde{\otimes}n$ the image of $m\otimes n$ under the natural maps $M\otimes N\rightarrow M\otimes_{K}N\rightarrow M\widetilde{\otimes}N.$ The subspace of the topological tensor product spanned by all elements of this form is dense in $M\widetilde{\otimes}N.$ The usual associativity and commutativity constraints induce the following K-linear isomorphisms

$$
(M \widetilde {\otimes} N) \widetilde {\otimes} P \cong M \widetilde {\otimes} (N \widetilde {\otimes} P),
$$

(3.1)

$$
M \widetilde {\otimes} N \cong N \widetilde {\otimes} M.
$$

(3.2)

We also have

$$
K \widetilde {\otimes} M \cong \widetilde {M} \cong M \widetilde {\otimes} K,
$$

(3.3)

which means that K serves as a unit for completions.

The topological tensor product is functorial as can be seen from the definition: if $f : M \to M^{\prime}$ and $g : N \to N^{\prime}$ are K-linear maps, then there exists a K-linear map

$$
f \widetilde {\otimes} g: M \widetilde {\otimes} N \rightarrow M ^ {\prime} \widetilde {\otimes} N ^ {\prime}
$$

enjoying the formal properties of the algebraic tensor product.

Proposition XVI.3.2. If M and N are topologically free modules, then so is $M\widetilde{\otimes} N$ . More precisely, we have

$$
V [ [ h ] ] \widetilde {\otimes} W [ [ h ] ] = (V \otimes W) [ [ h ] ].
$$

PROOF. For any K-module M, the natural maps

$$
V [ [ h ] ] \widetilde {\otimes} W [ [ h ] ] = (V \otimes W) [ [ h ] ].
$$

PROOF. For any K-module M, the natural maps

$$
M \otimes_ {K} K _ {n} \rightarrow M \otimes_ {K} K / h ^ {n} K \rightarrow M / h ^ {n} M
$$

are isomorphisms, where the first one is induced by (1.4) and the second one is given by $m\otimes f\mapsto fm$ (the inverse map being induced by $m\mapsto m\otimes 1 )$ Applying this to $M\otimes_{K} N$ where $M=V[[h]]$ and $N=W[[h]]$ we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} (M \otimes_ {K} N) / h ^ {n} (M \otimes_ {K} N) \cong (M \otimes_ {K} N) \otimes_ {K} K _ {n} \\ \cong \left(M \otimes_ {K} K _ {n}\right) \otimes_ {K _ {n}} \left(N \otimes_ {K} K _ {n}\right) \\ \cong M / h ^ {n} M \otimes_ {K _ {n}} N / h ^ {n} N \\ \cong \left(V \otimes K _ {n}\right) \otimes_ {K _ {n}} \left(W \otimes K _ {n}\right) \\ \cong (V \otimes W) \otimes K _ {n} \\ \cong (V \otimes W) [ [ h ] ] / h ^ {n} (V \otimes W) [ [ h ] ]. \\ \end{array}
$$

Passing to the inverse limit yields the desired result.
